/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shootin.headline: Seven planes across Europe searched or diverted after ‘malicious hoax’ bomb threats
/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shootin.excerpt: Seven planes across Europe have been searched or diverted after a series of bomb threats were made to passenger flights, prompting questions as to whether there was any coordination behind the warnings. Two UK departures – one from Heathrow and one from Manchester – were among those threatened in what Downing Street called “malicious hoaxes”, though all planes landed safely and no explosives were found. A UK Department for Transport source added that the low-level threats were “not credible” and that passengers should not be concerned, though the warnings disrupted flights and prompted investigations across the UK and Europe. None of the incidents and subsequent searches threw up any evidence of terrorist activity, though authorities were responding to an unusual number of reported threats in one day. One of Warsaw’s two main airports, Modlin, was briefly closed after receiving a diverted plane, and Polish officials confirmed that they had received bomb threats involving two flights coming into the capital. Italian fighter jets escorted a Ryanair plane into Rome following a warning of a suspected threat on a flight coming from Dublin. The flight landed safely and nothing untoward was reported as being found. There was little obvious pattern surrounding the incidents, which affected flights taking off from the UK, Ireland, Denmark, Portugal and Italy, and landing in Poland, Spain, Italy and Bulgaria.
/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shootin.trail: Unclear if series of incidents affecting two UK departures and several Ryanair services, among others, were connected

/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shootin.headline: Tusk defends overhaul of Poland’s constitutional court despite protests
/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shootin.excerpt: Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has vowed to see through a contested overhaul of the country’s constitutional court, declaring that “in certain matters, there can be no compromise”. In a prime-time television address on Saturday night, Tusk was defiant, despite overnight protests that saw riot police drafted to protect the court’s building, saying the shake-up was vital to restore a tribunal crippled by years of political disputes. Paralysed for more than a decade, the court sat at the core of rule of law clashes between the rightwing Law and Justice (PiS) party and the EU during the party’s eight-year rule. Since returning to office in 2023, the centre-right Tusk has sought to unwind those judicial changes, but his agenda has been frustrated by opposition-aligned presidents with extensive veto powers. Earlier this year, president Karol Nawrocki refused to swear in five judges approved by parliament. The crisis flared again on Friday when a group of government-backed judges attempted to seize procedural control of the tribunal, suspending the PiS-appointed chief judge and deputy and prompting street protests. Defending the action, Tusk said “there was never any doubt that the court in the form imposed by PiS was not a genuine court”, citing adverse rulings from European tribunals. He compared the opposition outrage to “a thief snatching an elderly woman’s handbag, running off, and when he is caught, he screams that he is subjected to violence”.
/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shootin.trail: Prime minister says shake-up is vital to restore tribunal crippled by years of political disputes

/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shootin.headline: Riot police deployed to Poland’s constitutional court after judge suspended
/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shootin.excerpt: Riot police were locked in a tense standoff with protesters outside Poland’s constitutional court on Friday night after its top judge was suspended in the latest escalation in a decade-long dispute over the court’s legal status. The clashes followed a controversial decision by a group of government-appointed judges to suspend the court’s contested president, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, amid disagreements over the bench’s legitimacy. The move prompted a furious reaction from the rightwing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, with its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, condemning what he claimed was an “assault” on the court. The court frequently ruled in favour of Polish legislation over EU law and the European Union accused Poland’s highest court of being too close to the nationalist political power of the time. The PiS-backed conservative president, Karol Nawrocki, a close ally of Donald Trump, turned his plane around en route to a state visit in Senegal to return to Warsaw and intervene at the court on Friday night. Hundreds of protesters – including opposition MPs – gathered outside the building to show their support for the suspended judges. Police said they detained three people after some protesters breached the tribunal’s fence and others threw objects at officers.
/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shootin.trail: President Karol Nawrocki seen struggling to gain entry to court building in Warsaw amid long-running row over the court’s legitimacy

/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shootin.headline: Poland’s parliament votes to ease abortion ban but faces likely veto from president
/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shootin.excerpt: Poland’s lower house of parliament has approved two bills aimed at loosening a near-total ban on abortions, in what campaigners have described as a “small-scale step” ahead of protests calling on the government to fulfil its promises to overhaul the country’s laws. The new measures, which are likely to be vetoed by Poland’s nationalist president, would remove some of the criminal penalties for those who help women to access abortion care and allow terminations in cases of foetal abnormalities. Leah Hoctor, of the Center for Reproductive Rights, said: “These bills represent a very small-scale change. Even if these pieces of legislation are ratified and signed into law by the Polish president – which remains to be seen – they would change very little for most women in Poland who need abortion care.” This view was echoed by the NGO Legalna Aborcja (Legal Abortion), a reproductive rights and advocacy initiative. “What does this mean for women who need an abortion right now? Nothing, because none of these bills would help them,” said a spokesperson. The Fundacja Widzialne (Visible Foundation) asked people to keep up the pressure on the government by taking to the streets on Thursday. “Poland still has an inhumane abortion law,” it wrote on social media as it announced rallies in 27 cities.
/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shootin.trail: Measures would remove some penalties for those helping women access abortion but are ‘small-scale step’, say campaigners

/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shootin.headline: Poland’s ascent from communist state to top 20 economy reverses the brain drain
/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shootin.excerpt: Above the rain-soaked streets of Warsaw, the observation deck of the Varso tower overlooks Joseph Stalin’s gift to Poland that has divided opinion for decades. For some, the Soviet-era Palace of Culture and Science is a drunk confectioner’s nightmare; standing as a relic of oppression that should have been demolished. For others, it is an icon on the skyline and a monumental warning from history. For the managers of the Varso – completed four years ago, as the tallest building in the EU – with its 310m-high spire rising symbolically above its Stalinist neighbour, it is a waypoint on Poland’s rapid path to economic prosperity. “We look down on it,” says Cezary Błaszczyk, the managing director of HB Reavis in Poland, which owns the tower, gesturing at the palace opposite. A few months ago a slackline walker traversed the 500m gap between the buildings. “It was a symbolic walk from the past to the future,” says his colleague Natalia Kasperska. “Since we are higher and taller than the Palace of Culture, we treat it as: ‘We got over communism, and now we are a country with a strong economy,’” Błaszczyk says. Over the four decades since regaining its independence from Soviet-dominated rule, Poland has been transformed. Excluding oil-exporting states and financial hubs, incomes have converged with western levels at the fastest rate in the world; from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year.
/world/2026/nov/07/krakow-poland-shootin.trail: In the final part of our series on the country, Poles tell how wages have soared – along with the cost of living

/world/2026/nov/07/israel-president-gadi.headline: US midterm results may help unite Israeli coalition to unseat Netanyahu
/world/2026/nov/07/israel-president-gadi.excerpt: The Democrats’ sweep of Congress may make it easier for Israel’s splintered opposition to overcome deep internal divisions and form a coalition government, by increasing the urgency of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu, who has associated himself so closely with Donald Trump’s Republicans. But as Israel took stock of the results, there was also a sense that the elections marked a longer-term shift in US politics that will make the job of any new Israeli leader far more difficult. The United States provides Israel with critical military and diplomatic support, so nurturing bipartisan ties was the cornerstone of foreign policy for decades. Netanyahu ripped up that commitment to throw his lot in with the Republicans in general and Trump in particular. The opposition had always attacked his decision as ill-judged. By the end of the week, they were warning that it was positively dangerous. “These people aren’t against Israel,” prominent opposition politician Yair Lapid said of incoming Democratic lawmakers, urging his country to rebuild bridges. “They’re mainly against Netanyahu – for them, anything connected to him is toxic.” “The easiest thing is to scream that ‘America is lost,’ because if it’s lost, you don’t have to work. That’s just not true. Not at all.” Lapid laid out a plan to “rebuild trust” in the US, but it perhaps did more to demonstrate the scale of the problem than reassure Israelis.
/world/2026/nov/07/israel-president-gadi.trail: Democrats’ sweep could urge Israel’s divided opposition to join forces and remove prime minister closely allied with Trump

/world/2026/nov/07/israel-president-gadi.headline: ‘Wrong on every count’: How the Guardian reported the 1956 Suez crisis
/world/2026/nov/07/israel-president-gadi.excerpt: On 26 July 1956, Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser announced the nationalisation of the Suez Canal Company, the joint British-French enterprise which had owned and operated the canal since its construction in 1869. Both countries saw this as a threat to their interests and responded with a coordinated attack (with Israel) to take back the canal zone. Israeli forces swept into the Sinai desert on 29 October and two days later there was an Anglo-French bombing campaign against Egyptian military targets. But on 6 November, under intense pressure from the international community and particularly the US, Britain and France accepted a UN-mandated ceasefire. The Manchester Guardian was against the use of force from the beginning of the crisis. Under newly appointed editor Alastair Hetherington, the paper condemned an ultimatum given to the Egyptians to withdraw from the canal as “an act of folly without justification,” and on 5 November described the actions as “hideously miscalculated and utterly immoral”. The Guardian’s critical coverage of the invasion proved so uncomfortable for the prime minister, Anthony Eden, that he tried to prevent the BBC from quoting from it and wanted the paper’s diplomatic correspondent, Richard Scott, banned from the airwaves.
/world/2026/nov/07/israel-president-gadi.trail: The military conflict in Egypt involving the UK, France and Israel that ended with a humiliating exit for the two European nations

/world/2026/nov/07/israel-president-gadi.headline: Food grown in illegal West Bank settlements being sold in Australia as ‘produce of Israel’
/world/2026/nov/07/israel-president-gadi.excerpt: Millions of dollars of food grown in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank has been shipped to Australia labelled as “produce of Israel”, a new analysis of trade data has shown. The human rights legal organisation Global Echo has analysed commercial documents and official trade data from the Israeli government and the Australian Bureau of Statistics, showing at least US$5m (A$7.2m) of organic dates grown in illegal settlements across the West Bank have been shipped to Australia over the past eight years. Global Echo analysed 132 agricultural shipments from Israel to Australia between August 2018 and August 2026. Of those, 85 – or 64% – contained settlement products. The proportion of settlement goods is higher in more recent years. Between January 2025 and August 2026, 20 of 24 shipments of dates to Australia analysed by Global Echo were sourced from settlements. Israel’s settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law. The settlements where dates bound for Australia are grown – including Netiv Hagdud, Beit Haarava, Arvot Jericho, Hamra, Tomer, Mechora, and Naaran – are occupied parts of the West Bank, recognised as part of the state of Palestine by Australia. Israeli law obliges exports to label the origin of products from settlements as being from Israel, unless they are being exported to a country with laws that prohibit such labelling.
/world/2026/nov/07/israel-president-gadi.trail: Analysis by human rights organisation Global Echo shows 85 of 132 shipments over eight years contained more than US$5m of organic dates grown in settlements

/world/2026/nov/07/israel-president-gadi.headline: The midterms were a thumping rebuke of the US-Israel relationship
/world/2026/nov/07/israel-president-gadi.excerpt: On the eve of a midterm election that ended in an unequivocal rejection of his brand of politics, even Donald Trump seemed to recognize that the US-Israel relationship had become a political liability. Trump’s 11th-hour suggestion, on election morning, that he would cut military aid to Israel at the end of the year because, as he put it, “they don’t need it”, was condemned across the board – with pro-Palestinian advocates dismissing it as “desperate” and pro-Israel ones as “unserious”. Trump’s suggestion that he would replace nearly $4bn in annual military aid with arms sales signaled little would change in practice – the funding would continue and it would be harder to track. But it was still a notable recognition by the president of just how much support for Israel has tanked against the backdrop of the latest war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians, been widely described as a genocide, and reshaped US politics in ways unthinkable just three years ago. Indeed, come January, the US House will include an army doctor who went on a medical mission in Gaza, a lawyer who was fired by her firm over a blogpost criticizing Israel’s war, a Jewish lawmaker who was recently detained by Israeli forces while helping Palestinians harvest olives in the occupied West Bank, and a community organizer who participated in a pro-Palestine student encampment and scored one of the primary season’s most stunning upsets under the banner “babies, not bombs”.
/world/2026/nov/07/israel-president-gadi.trail: Even Trump seems to recognize that the relationship has become a political liability, and may never be the same

/world/2026/nov/07/israel-president-gadi.headline: Win or lose? Inside the 6 November Guardian Weekly
/world/2026/nov/07/israel-president-gadi.excerpt: I’m writing this as the world wakes up to news of a blue wave of Democrat wins in the US midterms. What they mean for America and the world will be the subject of next week’s issue but this week we are focusing on Israel. As seasoned Knesset watchers know, the plethora of parties on the ballot and proportional representation rarely produce immediate clear winners and a new government in short order. But as Jonathan Freedland puts it in this week’s cover story, the 2026 election presents a philosophical as well as a political puzzle. Benjamin Netanyahu may have lost his parliamentary majority, but the opposition bloc needs more than Jewish parties to take control of the Knesset and offer Gadi Eisenkot the premiership. As Jonathan explains, Netanyahu’s loss contains the path to a possible win, while the road to success for Eisenkot means working with Palestinian parties, a red line many Jewish voters and MPs may not be willing to cross. The real headline result so far is that Palestinian parties are now in a pivotal position and that Bedouin turnout was key to their winning an unprecedented 19 seats. As our Middle East correspondent, Emma Graham-Harrison, reports, women’s self-organisation led to up to 93% of eligible voters casting their ballots in some areas. This has given the Arab coalition a “historic” opportunity to change Israel’s direction.
/world/2026/nov/07/israel-president-gadi.trail: Who will control the Knesset? Plus: why the argument over autism?

/world/2026/nov/07/europe-leaders-call-c.headline: Home Office sued after stripping almost 1,500 EU citizens of right to live in UK
/world/2026/nov/07/europe-leaders-call-c.excerpt: The Home Office is being sued for alleged breach of the Brexit withdrawal agreement after stripping almost 1,500 EU citizens of their full rights to live in the UK. Campaign group the3million lodged papers at the high court on Friday after several cases emerged of EU citizens who were granted pre-settled status to remain in the country after Brexit but were told recently those decisions were an “error”. According to the statement of claim, the Home Office decision to remove all or some rights from citizens granted pre-settled status was made without “procedural protections” required under the Brexit withdrawal agreement (WA). These protections include a right of an appeal and an assessment of “proportionality”, which would establish whether removal of rights was appropriate given the EU citizens in question built their lives in the UK on the basis of the Home Office’s original decision. Among the people affected by the Home Office policy was a 33-year-old Brazilian Italian engineer who has been in London since 2018. He was originally told that he should not have settled status: he could stay but his Brazilian wife could not, a decision that was reversed in the last few weeks after objections were raised. Another EU citizen who raised her case with the3million is a woman working in the NHS and studying for a PhD in dentistry. She has said the Home Office’s notification had “turned her life upside down”.
/world/2026/nov/07/europe-leaders-call-c.trail: Campaign group the3million lodges court papers after EU citizens told pre-settled status was an ‘error’

/world/2026/nov/07/europe-leaders-call-c.headline: EU charges TikTok with failing to protect users’ mental health
/world/2026/nov/07/europe-leaders-call-c.excerpt: TikTok has been charged by the European Commission with failing to protect users’ mental health by exposing them to a relentless stream of content that risks worsening eating disorders and anxiety in a case that strikes at its business model. Issuing a preliminary ruling on Friday, the EU regulator said TikTok’s algorithm “can be harmful” and was leading young and vulnerable users “down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from”. The Chinese-owned short-video platform, which has 189 million users in the EU, was found to have failed to prevent users from being served up repetitive content on themes such as body image or isolation, which can lead to anxiety, sadness, worsen existing eating disorders or mental health problems. Officials said their investigation focused on legal content, where a single video might not be problematic, but the cumulative effect of watching scores of them on one theme could damage users’ mental health. TikTok’s safeguards to mitigate the risks of “rabbit-hole effects” – where users are served narrow and repetitive content to keep them engaged – were found to be ineffective. For example, officials said, if a user checked a “not interested” button on a video about eating patterns, the algorithm would still offer them similar content on diet and body image. Similarly, refreshing a feed only provided a brief respite from a stream of content on one topic, it found.
/world/2026/nov/07/europe-leaders-call-c.trail: Regulator’s initial ruling says algorithm ‘can be harmful’ and led young and vulnerable viewers ‘down rabbit holes they can’t easily escape’

/world/2026/nov/07/europe-leaders-call-c.headline: Denmark’s top court to rule on ‘parallel societies’ after ‘non-western’ people evicted
/world/2026/nov/07/europe-leaders-call-c.excerpt: Denmark’s supreme court is expected to rule on whether the state’s classification of residents with “non-western” backgrounds is covered by racial discrimination law. The appeal by residents who were evicted from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej in Helsingør, a city north of Copenhagen, could have far-reaching implications for others who have been forced out of their homes by the controversial legislation previously known as the “ghetto law”. The government now refers to affected neighbourhoods as “parallel societies”. The residents, who have been unsuccessful in other courts, argue that the evictions by the housing association were intended to cut the number of residents with a “non-western” background in order to stop the area from becoming a “ghetto” and therefore subject to the legislation. The government has previously argued the classification is unrelated to ethnicity. In December, the European court of justice (ECJ) ruled that the legislation may be unlawful. The law requires housing associations to cut not-for-profit housing by 40%, including by selling or demolishing properties or terminating the lease of tenants by 2030. It also includes demolishing apartment blocks in areas previously labelled “tough ghettos” (now “transformation areas”) by the government, where at least half of residents have a “non-western” background. Other areas with similar socioeconomic conditions – such as high levels of unemployment or crime – are not subject to these measures.
/world/2026/nov/07/europe-leaders-call-c.trail: Government claims removal of former residents of housing complex in Helsingør is unrelated to their ethnicity

/world/2026/nov/07/europe-leaders-call-c.headline: EU presses UK to guarantee discounted university tuition fees for European students
/world/2026/nov/07/europe-leaders-call-c.excerpt: The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European students discounted rates on university tuition fees before a much-anticipated summit this month. At a meeting of senior EU diplomats on Wednesday, at least six member states called for a clear commitment from the UK by the time of the summit that EU students will pay the lower domestic rate of university tuition fees. These member states oppose deferring agreement for another half-year. Many believe a failure to reach an agreement should delay the highly prized food and drink deal to cut Brexit red tape coming into force. European Commission negotiators have proposed postponing agreement on tuition fees by six months to ensure the success of the November event, where Burnham is expected to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU. Andy Burnham will meet the EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa on 20 November in Brussels, with the aim of signing three agreements – on food and drink, carbon markets and youth exchange – as well as pledging a “trusted partnership” on steel and defence industries. But a longstanding dispute over whether EU students should pay costly international tuition fees at British universities remains unresolved and could delay the implementation of the food and energy deals, which are worth billions to the British economy.
/world/2026/nov/07/europe-leaders-call-c.trail: Failure to agree lower fees for EU citizens studying in UK should delay prized food and drink deal, members say

/world/2026/nov/07/europe-leaders-call-c.headline: The UK-EU food produce deal: what was agreed and will it affect shoppers?
/world/2026/nov/07/europe-leaders-call-c.excerpt: The UK and the EU have finalised their deal to remove red tape for food producers and agreed first drafts on joint positions on migration, youth mobility and electricity trading before a summit on 20 November. The draft text of a joint statement has emerged 17 days before the summit, an indication of the consensual state of play between two sides previously at loggerheads during the Conservative government era. What is the overall deal on 20 November? The food deal is one of three main issues identified by the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer, for his “reset” of relations with the EU. Andy Burnham promised to stick with them and the focus on food, electricity and a youth travel scheme for British and EU citizens between 18 and 30 years old. What else is in the deal? “Cooperation built on strong foundations” is the title of the draft statement which sets out plans for deeper relations on migration, the possibility of a youth mobility scheme, continued joint support for Ukraine, furthering the strong defence and security relationship and cooperation on hybrid threats such as recent drone incidents at European airports linked to Russia. What are the practical implications of the food and drinks reset? The details announced on Tuesday mean exports of fresh meat, fish, shellfish and seed potatoes, largely from Scotland, can resume without costly paperwork proving they comply with EU standards.
/world/2026/nov/07/europe-leaders-call-c.trail: Two sides agree deal to remove some Brexit checks on food and animal product exports to EU

/us-news/2026/nov/07/stephen-miller-demo.headline: Judge to appoint special master to determine whether Trump lawyers purposely misled her over golf course
/us-news/2026/nov/07/stephen-miller-demo.excerpt: A federal judge said on Saturday that she intended to appoint an ex-top federal prosecutor who served during Donald Trump’s first term to investigate whether she was purposely misled by lawyers and administration officials over changes to a historic public golf course in Washington DC. Jessie Liu, a former US attorney for the District of Columbia, would examine whether officials with the interior department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Department of Justice violated ethics or misled US district judge Ana Reyes during the course of the civil case that was initiated with a lawsuit in February by the DC Preservation League and two golfers. The lawsuit challenges one of the US president’s flurry of construction projects around the nation’s capital – in this case, the renovation of a public golf facility along the Potomac River, which is less high-profile that some of his other plans but had still riled many. The Republican administration plans to close the East Potomac golf course and park on 15 November with the intention of constructing what it has called a “World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events”. An injunction issued by Reyes last month temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the course and ordered the administration to give 10 days’ notice in writing before making any “irreparable modification” to any “forms or features” of the course while the lawsuit is active.
/us-news/2026/nov/07/stephen-miller-demo.trail: Ana Reyes wants to know whether federal officials lied about extent of renovation plans at East Potomac golf course

/us-news/2026/nov/07/stephen-miller-demo.headline: Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller is a middle finger to millions of voters
/us-news/2026/nov/07/stephen-miller-demo.excerpt: Donald Trump just gave the middle finger to millions of American voters. Any other president who suffered the kind of drubbing at the polls that Trump did this week might have felt at least a sliver of humility – and perhaps even an obligation to work with the new opposition in Congress. But not for the first time in his political career, Trump veered in the opposite direction. On Friday he made Stephen Miller, condemned by Democrats and civil rights groups as a white nationalist, one of the most powerful unelected officials in Washington by naming him White House chief of staff. Miller is the architect of Trump’s far-right, nativist immigration agenda. He is, therefore, arguably the architect of the blue wave that engulfed Republicans in Tuesday’s midterm elections as voters – including many Latinos – expressed their disgust. Yet instead of firing Miller, Trump promoted him. It was a declaration of war. Miller, 41, is a longtime proponent of the presidential authority that Trump has spent the past two years expanding at the expense of Congress. In 2017 he declared: “The powers of the president to protect our country are very substantial and will not be questioned.” Now Republicans’ catastrophic defeat is likely to leave Trump more reliant on unilateral executive action than ever to advance his domestic agenda. “In a lot of ways Stephen Miller has been the id to Trump’s authoritarian impulses and machinations,” Kurt Bardella, an adviser to Democrats in Texas, said.
/us-news/2026/nov/07/stephen-miller-demo.trail: Architect of Trump’s far-right immigration agenda is now most powerful unelected figure in government – it suggests White House is moving to a war footing

/us-news/2026/nov/07/stephen-miller-demo.headline: Stephen Miller’s appointment shows Trump hasn’t learned his lesson on immigration
/us-news/2026/nov/07/stephen-miller-demo.excerpt: On Tuesday, US midterm voters resoundingly rebuked Donald Trump and his brutal mass deportation campaign that sent military tanks and masked agents though residential streets. But on Friday, the president doubled down. He named Stephen Miller – the architect of the administration’s most aggressive immigration policies – as his chief of staff. It was never likely that Trump – who rose to political prominence on the promise that he would expel immigrants en masse from the US – would dampen his agenda, even after voters rejected Republican candidates up and down the ballot, near and far from the southern border, in blue and deep-red states. But the elevation of Miller – a zealous, anti-immigrant crusader who has been by Trump’s side since the president’s first term – is an ominous signal that the deportation machine that Trump has built up over the past two years will be driving ahead at full speed. Miller more than any single other person is responsible for unleashing a series of violent immigration raids across US cities this year and last, for sending hordes of masked agents in military gear through residential streets to round up undocumented immigrants. He has pushed the administration to all but shut down legal immigration as well. In his previous roles – as a deputy chief of staff and policy adviser – he has stuck close to Trump’s side and stoked the president’s most extreme instincts.
/us-news/2026/nov/07/stephen-miller-demo.trail: US voters repudiated mass deportation campaign, but choice of new chief of staff is an ominous signal that Trump is driving ahead at full speed

/us-news/2026/nov/07/stephen-miller-demo.headline: Susie Wiles exits White House as Trump ousts another woman from key role
/us-news/2026/nov/07/stephen-miller-demo.excerpt: Donald Trump on Friday said Susie Wiles, the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, will leave her post, a major shake-up of his inner circle that comes amid a steady exodus of senior female officials from his administration. The president announced her ouster – and her replacement, by the immigration hardliner Stephen Miller – in a post on Truth Social, days after a sweeping blue wave gave Democrats control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections. Wiles’s departure leaves behind an overwhelmingly male leadership team. “I wanted to make a change,” he told reporters on Friday. “I think Susie’s done a very good job … Stephen’s been great and we’ve got to make moves.” Wiles, who reportedly handed in her resignation on Thursday night, said her role as chief of staff “has been the honor of a lifetime,” adding: “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together, from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America first.” Wiles’s exit follows a string of high-profile resignations and dismissals of women in the Trump administration. In recent months, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was ousted just five days after taking up the role, while former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem and former attorney general Pam Bondi were also dismissed.
/us-news/2026/nov/07/stephen-miller-demo.trail: Wiles thanks president for ‘honor of a lifetime’ as departure leaves behind overwhelmingly male leadership team

/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.headline: Russell Brand barrister reports himself to watchdog over clash with journalist
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.excerpt: Russell Brand’s barrister has reported himself to his professional regulator after being accused of launching a tirade at a journalist shortly after his client had been found guilty of rape. Ian Winter KC “confronted” the Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward, telling her: “I hope you are pleased with yourself.” Urwin responded: “I’m pleased justice has been done,” to which Winter replied: “Well, it wasn’t. You fucked it.” “Congratulations,” he added, in an incident that happened outside the courtroom door at Southwark crown court on Thursday afternoon, with a group of journalists watching. In a statement issued on Friday lunchtime, Winter said he had referred himself to the Bar Standards Board, his professional regulator. He said: “Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today’s press, I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny. “I have made such a report.” The incident happened moments after a jury had found Brand guilty of rape and three counts of sexual assault at the conclusion of a four-week trial. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault. Brand, 51, had denied all the charges against him, and argued through his lawyer that he had been wrongly accused and was the victim of a media conspiracy.
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.trail: Ian Winter KC told Rosamund Urwin of the Sunday Times, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward: ‘I hope you are pleased with yourself’

/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.headline: ‘He’s manipulating its power’: why did Russell Brand convert to Christianity?
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.excerpt: The women whom Russell Brand raped and sexually assaulted have for weeks endured the ordeal of a heavily publicised trial. Throughout, Brand held online prayer meetings with followers. Does he feel Christian sympathy for those women? Only Brand, in the deepest recesses of his conscience, can know. The answer would be the best indicator of whether the disgraced comic, actor and born-again Christian has worn his newfound faith as a cloak in an effort to deflect and distract from the seriousness of the allegations against him. Or whether his conversion is a profound and sincere one – a spiritual crutch he may need in the coming years. Whatever the truth, Brand’s case demonstrates how Christianity has become a frontier in the culture wars along which battle lines are now drawn on all kinds of ethical, political and even legal issues. It is not hard to see why Brand’s embrace of Christ has raised suspicion. His reputation for most of his career has been one of a hell-raiser, and even when spirituality did call, it was the eastern traditions of Buddhism and the Hare Krishna movement that first caught his eye. Now, latterly dedicated to the teachings of Christ, his very visible displays of devotion have at times seemed farcical. When Brand was interviewed by Piers Morgan in April, one moment went viral: Brand was asked to quote from a Bible that he was carrying with him – the same he took to the dock in Southwark crown court.
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.trail: Sincere or self-serving, the disgraced comedian’s case shows how the church became a culture war frontier

/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.headline: Flashbulbs, lies and victim blaming: how Russell Brand’s trial unfolded
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.excerpt: Russell Brand’s trial at Southwark crown court, which ended with him being found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others, was one of the most obsessively watched criminal cases in recent history. As well as Brand’s own conduct, the case became an examination of his victims’ evidence, the legal strategy his team used to defend him, and the culture within which he committed his crimes. The victims: ‘I remember him on me. I know I said no’ Brand’s victims told how he “snapped” from charming to nasty as he raped and sexually assaulted them before gaslighting them into believing nothing was wrong. The comedian’s youngest victim, who was 21 when he targeted her at the height of his fame in 2009, was left traumatised by their encounter. Brand had stored her name in his phone alongside a series of letters and symbols. The court heard the letter “T” stood for “tart”, while “AP” denoted anal play, and two asterisks meant: “Never, ever forget this individual, this is a memorable encounter.” It was, indeed, an encounter the woman would never forget, she spent years torturing and blaming herself for what happened. The woman was starstruck when she met Brand after one of his standup performances at the Hammersmith Apollo in early 2009. Brand, who was more than a decade her senior, picked the woman from the crowd and invited her to his dressing room. There, she performed oral sex on him and engaged in a threesome with another young fan.
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.trail: Level of interest in comedian’s case resulted in examination of affairs inside and outside the courtroom

/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.headline: Russell Brand faces ‘significant’ prison term for rape and sexual assault
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.excerpt: Russell Brand has been found guilty of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three other women, ending a years-long legal saga that has raised questions about how he was able to commit his crimes at the height of his fame. Brand, 51, was described during his trial as a ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator. He was convicted of raping a woman at his luxury London townhouse and of sexually assaulting women in front of his entourage at their workplaces, at a radio station and TV studio. The Hollywood actor turned online influencer was accused of gaslighting his victims after the attacks, and treating women as a “disposable commodity” and a “means to an end” to satisfy his voracious sexual appetite. It can now be revealed that Brand is under investigation for two further rape allegations and that the Metropolitan police have submitted files to the Crown Prosecution Service. Brand – who will be sentenced on Monday – stood outside the door of the dock shortly before the jury delivered their verdicts and looked at his wife, Laura, saying: “Laura, I love you.” Wearing a grey three-piece suit, he appeared to be praying in the dock before he was convicted of four offences on Thursday after a four-week trial at Southwark crown court. He had pleaded not guilty to three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999.
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.trail: Actor and comedian, 51, found guilty of raping a woman and assaulting three others

/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.headline: Misogyny and sexism of Russell Brand case have not gone away, TV insiders say
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.excerpt: Even within the culture of casual misogyny and sexism that pervaded the TV world in the mid-noughties, Naomi Harvey and her colleagues concluded they needed to do something about Russell Brand. Harvey was one of a team of researchers tasked with finding fans of Big Brother, Channel 4’s reality TV juggernaut, to appear on the discussion show Big Brother’s Big Mouth, hosted by Brand. They had noticed Brand’s habit of asking a runner, the most junior person on the production, to obtain the phone numbers of female audience members and pass them to him. But something new had just happened. A distraught audience member had phoned Harvey to complain after being invited for drinks by Brand after the show. “All I remember is being really taken aback that she was so upset,” Harvey recalled. “We noticed this behaviour of taking women’s numbers, and now it had escalated to the point that we’d had a member of the public phone up the desk upset. “We felt as the audience team we had a responsibility, so me and my two colleagues reported it up to our next boss. “We never heard anything again.” The episode is minor when set against the criminality exposed during Brand’s trial. Yet it is part of a culture that appeared to indulge Brand and fail to confront troubling behaviour. Brand’s case has led to difficult questions for the BBC, Channel 4 and the production companies that worked with him.
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.trail: Concerns remain that media industry is still failing to confront troubling behaviour

/football/2026/nov/07/nottingham-forest-.excerpt: Lampard will get warm welcome at Everton Nothing better encapsulates the dysfunction that was Everton under Farhad Moshiri than the idea that an unknown vandal with a can of spray paint could influence the club’s managerial direction. “Pereira out, Lampard in” they daubed on a wall at Goodison Park when it appeared Vítor Pereira was in line to replace Rafael Benítez in 2022. Alarmed by fan protests, the Everton board opted instead for Frank Lampard and, while his tenure ended 12 months later with the club immersed in another relegation battle, there will be appreciation for the Coventry manager when he makes a first visit to Hill Dickinson Stadium on Friday. The connection between Lampard and Evertonians was genuine and a factor in keeping the club up in 2022. Both parties will be glad to see the other emerging stronger from those troubled times. Jack Grealish, meanwhile, will again be absent for Everton after his recent disciplinary breach, although the manager, David Moyes, said: “We will be working again with Jack soon.” Andy Hunter Everton v Coventry City, Friday 8pm (all times GMT) Farke keeps it real as Leeds aim to stop slide Back in September, when Leeds thrashed Newcastle 4-1 at Elland Road, talk of European qualification filled the West Yorkshire airwaves. Since then Daniel Farke’s side have drawn three and lost two of their ensuing Premier League games, scoring just two goals along the way.

/football/2026/nov/07/nottingham-forest-.headline: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
/football/2026/nov/07/nottingham-forest-.excerpt: Arsenal show maturity and quality Good defending is the mark of champions. At Anfield, where Arsenal had not won in the past 13 visits, Mikel Arteta followed the orthodoxy of locking down once his team took the lead. This time around, it proved successful. Arsenal did not allow the occasion or the stadium to get to them as they have on previous occasions. In April 2023, Granit Xhaka entangling with Trent Alexander-Arnold energised home fans previously despondent that Arsenal were 2-0 up. It finished 2-2. On Sunday, Liverpool zipped around zestfully, as Andoni Iraola requests, though the final-ball quality was lacking. That owed a great deal to the organisation of the Arsenal defence. Ahead of the last international break, Brighton set a blueprint for getting the better of Arsenal in winning 3-0. Liverpool’s squad profile might have made a similar strategy possible though Iraola’s outfit is struggling to create chances in the same volume as Brighton or his Bournemouth team. John Brewin Match report: Liverpool 0-1 Arsenal Reds’ attacking flurries not enough No shots on target for Liverpool, leaving them with zero margin for the errors that preceded Kai Havertz’s decisive goal. Nine points behind Arsenal with a quarter of the season gone, Liverpool’s season risks becoming a developmental one, a time to regroup and rethink rather than challenging for the title. The squad Iraola inherited still bears the weight of the failed rebuild of the summer of 2025.

/football/2026/nov/07/nottingham-forest-.headline: Should Premier League strugglers stick or twist as pressure on managers mounts?
/football/2026/nov/07/nottingham-forest-.excerpt: No Premier League manager has yet lost his job this season. In only three of the past 10 campaigns was November reached without a club making a managerial change. The 2026-27 season commencing with 11 managers who were appointed at some point in 2026 has probably contributed to the early season stability. They have to be given a chance to fashion their side as they see fit. But with roughly a quarter of the season played and only one more round of fixtures before an international break, the first sacking may not be far away. Michael Carrick remains the favourite to be the next manager to leave his post. He is unsurprisingly followed by the managers of the clubs who occupy the relegation zone: Pierre Sage of Crystal Palace, Sunderland’s Régis Le Bris and Oliver Glasner at Nottingham Forest. It seems almost inevitable that Carrick will leave soon so the more interesting analysis lies among the bottom three. Sunderland sit 20th and are predicted by Opta to finish there. However, they have had a testing start to the season. Le Bris’s side have faced five of the current top seven clubs, the joint-most along with Liverpool. The manager also has enormous reserves of goodwill after taking the club back to the Premier League and then into Europe. Despite their tough schedule, Sunderland came into the weekend within one expected point of Chelsea, Manchester United and Tottenham before losing 3-1 at Coventry with the xG count 1.8 to 0.7 in their favour.
/football/2026/nov/07/nottingham-forest-.trail: Unusually, all clubs in the top flight have the same manager with whom they began the season – but the first sacking may not be far away

/football/2026/nov/07/nottingham-forest-.headline: ‘I’m not here to be liked’: Glasner defiant as Brentford capitalise on Forest woes
/football/2026/nov/07/nottingham-forest-.excerpt: For Oliver Glasner and Nottingham Forest, the future starts now. His post-match press conference lasted 14 frustrated minutes in which, repeatedly banging the desk, he blamed himself for compromising his principles and told players that if they didn’t “buy in” they could “leave”. “For me, I go home and have breakfast with my family, so it’s not the worst situation,” Glasner said. “Nobody needs to have pity with Oliver Glasner. If I want, I could start in two weeks somewhere else. I won’t do it. But the players, the staff, they remain in the same situation. And it’s the same shit situation that the club had last year. So you need to change and rebuild from the bottom to the top. And this is clear for me. And this is what I will do. And without any compromises, zero, zero.” Forest, once again, didn’t play too badly. No side has underperformed their xG as significantly as Forest, who went into the weekend third in Opta’s expected table but third-bottom in real life. Here, they had two-and-a-half times as many chances as Brentford. They could claim a degree of misfortune in that both goals went in off the luckless Nikola Milenkovic, the first an own goal after Murillo had misjudged a long clearance to Dango Ouattara, the second credited to Igor Thiago as he latched on to Jaydon Anthony’s clever low cross. But Glasner was accepting no excuses. “It’s not anger,” he said. “It’s necessary.” The result, Glasner said, was “disappointing and frustrating.
/football/2026/nov/07/nottingham-forest-.trail: Nottingham Forest were made to pay for a string of missed chances as Brentford won 2-0, their first Premier League win since before the international break

/music/2026/nov/07/richard-lloyd-punk-ba.headline: ‘I could get laid every night of the week!’: punk icon Legs McNeil on booze, benders and dating Sinéad O’Connor
/music/2026/nov/07/richard-lloyd-punk-ba.excerpt: Legs McNeil vividly remembers the reaction he got from the original CBGB bands in 1975 when they heard the name of the magazine he co-founded: Punk, the first publication ever dedicated to the form. “Absolutely no one wanted to be called a punk back then,” he said. “Not even the Ramones. Johnny Ramone demanded that we cross out every reference to punk in an article about them.” Flash forward a few years and, “suddenly everybody wanted to be called a punk!” McNeil said. “The Ramones started running around telling everyone, ‘you know, we were the first punk band!’” No doubt McNeil had something to do with that. After all, his affinity for the punk attitude and ethos ran so deep, he received billing in the magazine as its “resident punk”. As an illustration-heavy publication that was driven by the zany art of the magazine’s co-creator John Holmstrom, each issue presented McNeil as a consummately sly and seedy cartoon character, instantly transforming him into a real-life answer to Mad Magazine’s mascot of snark, Alfred E Neuman. “My only qualification was that I was this huge fuck-up,” McNeil said. “I was barely literate and I wasn’t much of a writer at the time. But I was that guy.” In a way, he still is.
/music/2026/nov/07/richard-lloyd-punk-ba.trail: As he releases a tell-all book, the Punk magazine founder and self-described ‘fuck-up’ holds forth on 1970s excess, the American roots of punk and why the Beatles are ‘stupid’
